#4224. Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 Goes Nuclear Against ‘Lobby Shopping’

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

Players have used third-party applications to assist their play for years now, to mixed success and intent. Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

After unjustly banning a Battlefield 6 player, EA lost a court case to keep the ban in place.

Call of Duty: Warzone players have been utilizing one of the oddest forms of cheating I’ve ever heard of, peeking at the skill level of everyone in the lobby through the app Warzone Agent to decide whether or not to just leave the game. Activision has announced they’re clamping down hard on the practice, looking to eliminate it going forward.

Call of Duty players have been complaining about the franchise’s skill-based matchmaking (SBMM) for years now, a system where players are matched against foes equivalent to their skill level. This is, of course, how most matchmaking systems work, but COD players have been asking for its elimination since the original Modern Warfare remake.

In order to avoid these close matches, they utilize apps like Warzone Agent to figure out the average rank of the lobby before deciding to play, a practice Warzone’s anti-cheat division, Ricochet, has officially stood against. In their release surrounding the practice of lobby shopping, “moving forward, players who leave Warzone Agent loaded will not be able to access Multiplayer modes.”

Lobby shopping is the practice of hopping around warm-up stage lobbies to search for one with a lower skill ceiling, essentially targeting worse players to maximize your own boons. Activision has made it clear they won’t stand to suffer the practice any longer, further saying, “using unauthorized software to manipulate the player experience violates Activision Terms of Use and leaves your account and hardware subject to enforcement.”

Many benign apps for games like League and Valorant give easier access to community info, while other, more malicious cheats can completely ruin a game for everyone else in the lobby.

Threatening to drop the ban hammer on violators is a great way to shake the practice off, and Activision isn’t stopping there, clarifying what it considers cheating. That includes external account boosting, led by swarms of bots they’ve managed to start stomping out.

Bots plague any free-to-play game people want to put time into, and focusing more on curtailing them is a great step toward slowing the flow, even if it is just a bandage over the wound. For now, Activision has drawn their line in the sand. The only question is whether or not they’ll flinch in the face of community complaints, but they’ve stuck by their guns this long.

The community complaint around skill-based matchmaking has always struck me as incredibly odd, with these players mostly desiring a true random selection process. These random matches are, on paper, more varied, but in practice lead to matches that are total stomps for one side or the other, leaving plenty of players with a bad taste in their mouths.

Getting to be the one stomping can be great fun, but that’s also possible against players of your skill level. SBMM’s main purpose is to minimize the games that feel like complete wipes from the loser’s perspective, keeping them playing against those who are actually equivalent to them on a broad scale. It’s far from perfect, but it's better than literally just tossing a random selection of players in a room.

Without it, not only would many casual players have to gamble on getting crushed every other game, but Activision could lose those players after enough rough matches, the true reason for the practice’s continued support. Despite the complaints, Activision has clearly long since decided that skill-based matchmaking is the best middle ground for skilled and casual players alike, giving everyone designated lobbies where they’re at least promised matches that are competitive.

Modern Warfare 4's launch party is still going, with a free play period for DMZ ready to rake in new players.

A new teaser trailer for Death Stranding Isolations, an upcoming animated series coming exclusively to Disney+ and Hulu next year, premiered during Kojima Productions’ 10th Anniversary Exhibition Beyond the Strand. The series was first announced last year.

Death Stranding Isolations tells an original story in the Death Stranding universe set immediately after the events of the first game. #4222. Diablo 4’s Warlock looks like an unhinged Necromancer with Sorcerer energy in first look at gameplay

Diablo 4's practitioner of forbidden arts, The Warlock, has been officially unveiled as the second class coming with Lord of Hatred.

Thanks to a meaty, well-produced Diablo 4 Developer Update, we got to have our promised first look at gameplay of the Warlock, the second of two classes coming to the game with the upcoming Lord of Hatred expansion.

The showcase offered a deep look at the Warlock’s core archetypes, its gameplay and skills loop, and where the class sits within the game’s existing roster of diverse classes.

Since the initial reveal of Lord of Hatred, The Warlock has remained the mysterious second class. Anyone who pre-purchased the expansion was able to get immediate access to The Paladin, the other class arriving with the expansion. It wasn’t until February that Blizzard officially revealed the class to the world, but we had to wait until this most recent Developer Update to actually see it in action.

The Warlock’s pragmatism exists as the counterpart to The Paladin's purity, in that Warlocks don’t shy away from harnessing the powers of Hell to eliminate their enemies. The class can conjure up demons to do their bidding, and utilise attacks previously only available to legions of Hell.

The Warlock is a hybrid pet and caster class. Their gameplay revolves around summoning demons, and undermining enemies with shadow arts. They rely on two resources: Wrath, and Dominance. Casting Skills consumes Wrath, whereas Dominance is what allows the Warlock to summon and exploit demons.

The Warlock has four archetypes players can spec into. Legions are traditional summoners who rely on overwhelming numbers to crush enemies. Vanguards are closer to Sorcerers, capable of dealing damage head-on. Masterminds utilise shadowcraft to slowly drain their enemies. Finally, Ritualists are summoners of the most terrifying Hell demons.

The Warlock is able to do this by fusing Soul Shards into their bodies. Going down any of the four paths becomes available after reaching level 30, which is when the class mechanic is unlocked. Each Soul Shard is tied to a certain demon, and its through that power that the Warlock is able to call upon them in combat. Your choice does, of course, affect your abilities going forward.

Warlocks arrive alongside new Uniques that cater to their specific playstyles, which is similar to what we’ve previously seen with The Paladin, and The Spiritborn before that.

Lord of Hatred arrives April 28. While we wait, Diablo 4’s next season is kicking off next week to deliver a bit of mindless fun to hold us over until the big day.

#4221. EA Reportedly Closed BioWare To Invest In Developing Star Wars Battlefront III Instead Of The Next Mass Effect

Electronic Arts shut down the legendary RPG studio BioWare last week, ending development on an untitled fifth Mass Effect game. Since then, we've seen what appears to be a leaked trailer for the game, which suggests it might have been called Mass Effect Universe, and heard a sneak peek at what Grammy-winning composer Austin Wintory was cooking up for the beloved sci-fi RPG series. Over the past week, fans across the internet have tried to piece together how a publisher could decide to shut down a studio as prolific as BioWare, but according to a new Bloomberg report, the answer is Star Wars.

More specifically, Bloomberg writes that, presented with the opportunity to develop Star Wars Battlefront III with Disney, the publisher, which went private last year after a $55 billion acquisition,  chose to invest its money into that instead of BioWare's in-development Mass Effect sequel. The publication writes that EA looked at its portfolio for the coming years and had two massive sci-fi investments it could continue: Star Wars Battlefront III or BioWare's next Mass Effect. Even though Mass Effect was well into development, and even though the Battlefront threequel hasn't even entered development, EA chose to continue with the latter. And so BioWare was shut down, and Mass Effect development ended, though Bloomberg's sources say there are other, less significant reasons the studio was shuttered, too.

Those other factors include the poor reception to 2017's Mass Effect: Andromeda, the failure of Anthem in 2019, and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which, despite garnering positive critical reception, apparently missed EA's sales expectations by 50%.

There's also the uncomfortable reality that BioWare made progressive LGBTQIA+ positive games but was a studio within a publisher house now partially owned by the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, a government fund from a country where same-sex activity, including marriage, is criminalized, sometimes punishable by death; these harsh laws extend to other facets of the LGBTQIA+ community. Another investment partner in this acquisition of EA is Affinity Partners, a Miami-based investment firm founded and run by former White House senior advisor Jared Kushner, who is the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, a political figure who imposes laws that discriminate against the LGBTQIA+ community, especially the 1% of Americans who are transgender; Trump has also been known to mock this community in various ways. No official statements say BioWare shut down because of its progressive leanings, but one has to wonder if that was a factor, especially after reports that BioWare scrubbed diversity from demos to avoid negative feedback from EA (thanks, Kotaku).

When BioWare closed last week, only 50 employees remained, all working on the next Mass Effect, after years of layoffs at the studio.

A Mass Effect TV series is still in the works at Amazon, even though EA seems to have hung up Commander Shepard's video game suit for good.

#4220. Where To Find Every Magic Bean Location In The Ocarina Of Time Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has been released, which means it's time to do a bunch of side quests for Hyrule's strangest citizens. One of the easiest side activities to overlook is collecting and planting the ten Magic Beans in the soft soil spots throughout the map.

Since you will need these Magic Beans if you want to collect all the Gold Skulltulas and Pieces of Heart, here is a breakdown of where to find all ten so you can ensure you don't miss anything when exploring Hyrule.

To get the Magic Beans, you need to be Young Link, as the seller doesn't exist when you're an adult. Once you're in the past, head to Zora's River and look for a large, bald man sitting near the broken gate. Speaking with the Bean Seller, you will learn that he is, well, selling ten Magic Beans; however, the price for these will really drain you of Rupees.

The price for one Magic Bean will start out costing 10 Rupees, with each subsequent one increasing in price by an additional 10 Rupees. This means if you want to buy all of the Magic Beans, you need a whopping 550 Rupees. Of course, you do not need to buy them all at once, so it can be beneficial to keep picking up Magic Beans as you progress through the game.

Once you have a Magic Bean, look for a Bug Hole location and approach it. Equip the Magic Bean and then use this item while standing next to the soil to plant a flower. Remember, each of these Bug Holes also produces a Gold Skulltula if you drop an insect from a bottle on top of it. Make sure to do this so you can collect the Gold Skulltula Token, then plant the Magic Bean into the soft soil.

Remember, all this can only be done as Young Link, as those planted Magic Beans will sprout into colorful flowers you can ride to previously inaccessible locations.

Here is where to sell all of the Happy Mask Shopkeeper's masks in The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake.

Remember, there are a total of ten Magic Bean spots. You can only plant the Magic Beans as a child; however, some areas you will need to open up first as an adult before returning as a child. That being said, eight of the ten can be accessed before you even pull the Master Sword out of the Temple of Time.

The first Magic Bean location is right next to the Bean Seller. Directly to the right of the vendor, you will find a Magic Bean spot that you can use to reach the central ruins as an adult, where you can both reach a Gold Skulltula that spawns along the cliff walls and the Piece of Heart if you didn't snag it as Young Link.

Your next Magic Bean spot can be found at Lake Hylia, just to the left of the Lakeside Laboratory's main door. Using this Magic Bean Flower will take you around the lake as an adult, allowing you to access the fishing area without the Scarecrow Song. It will also take you to the Laboratory Roof, where you can use the ladder to reach a Piece of Heart at the top.

Magic Bean spot number three is located way back in Kokiri Forest. When you arrive, go to the store where you purchased the Deku Shield. Behind the store, to the right of the door, you will find a soft soil spot in the brush and grass. Using this flower will take you up to a spot with a single Purple Rupee and several Green Rupees.

One of two Magic Bean spots in the Lost Woods. From the Kokiri Forest entrance, go Left and then Left again. When you enter, look directly to your left, and you will see the bug hole where you can plant the bean. This flower will take you to a small chest which contains a Purple Rupee.

The next Magic Bean location is also in the Lost Woods. From the Kokiri Forest entrance, go Right, Left, Right, Left, and Left to enter a small grove with two Business Scrubs. Defeat them both, and you'll find a soil spot to the right where you can plant a Magic Bean. Riding this flower as an adult will bring you to a Gold Skulltula spawn location above you.

Upon entering Kakariko Graveyard, take the first two sets of stairs directly in front of you and then go to the left by the tree. You'll find the Magic Bean spot along the stone wall. This will give you a flower as an adult that you can ride to reach a Piece of Heart in the ruins above you.

For this Magic Bean spot, make your way up the Death Mountain Trail to the entrance of Dodongo's Cavern. Just inside the entrance, to the right, you will find a soft soil spot. Taking this flower will bring you to the top of Dodongo's Cavern's entrance, where you will find a Piece of Heart.

This one is a little trickier to obtain, as you'll need to progress through the story until you reach the entrance to the Fire Temple as Adult Link. When you do, Sheik will teach him the Bolero of Fire song, allowing you to warp to this spot in Death Mountain Crater. Now, use your ocarina to warp back to the Temple of Time and switch to Young Link. Play the Bolero of Fire as Young Link to go back to this spot and go to the soft soil spot directly behind you next to the crest of the Fire Temple on the ground. Remember, you won't have the Goron Tunic as a child, so work fast to avoid burning to death. Then return to this spot as an adult to find a flower that will take you to a Piece of Heart.

The most unnecessary Magic Bean Flower. Go to Gerudo Valley as a child and jump down into the river below near the waterfall. Swim to the stairs that lead to the area where the Gerudo warrior is tending to her cow. At the end of this path, near the rocky wall, you will find the ninth soft soil spot. Using this Magic Bean Flower will take you to a hidden Piece of Heart behind the nearby waterfall, but you can just go here as a child, making this a bit redundant.

The final Magic Bean spot is located in the Evil Desert Colossus right outside the Spirit Temple entrance. Just like the Death Mountain Crater one, you need to reach here as an adult and learn the Requiem of Spirit song from Sheik. Once they've taught you the song, go back to the Temple of Time, become a child, and play this new tune to teleport to the Spirit Temple entrance. To the left of the door into the temple will be the soft soil spot. Using this flower as an adult allows you to reach both a Gold Skulltula spawn point on one of the large rocks in the desert and a Piece of Heart!

There's a third unrevealed amiibo for the Ocarina of Time remake, and the NPC dialogue attached has fans asking some very pertinent questions.

We want to hear from you. Share your perspective in the comments below, and please keep the conversation respectful.

#4219. The Top 10 Best Horror Games To Play This Halloween

Humans are drawn to horror in all forms, real life and fiction. Perhaps it’s the desire to get as close to death as possible without actually dying; perhaps it’s the morality of life and knowing death comes for all of us; perhaps all our heads are just a little miswired. Whatever the reason, we flock to movies where supernatural entities and puppets on tricycles upend otherwise lovely lives, TV shows where murderous cults kill and stump local detectives, and books where the words on the page seem to follow you to bed. Games, however, go a step further, letting you enter the horror and control it (or become its victim), and you could argue that, as a result, they’re the most immersive form of fiction.

We at Game Informer love a healthy dose of horror from time to time, and we often review games like this. Some terrify us. Others… don’t. And the best ones stick with us for years and years after the credits. Below is a list of 10 of the best horror games we’ve played recently. This isn’t an all-time list, so don’t fret if your personal favorite isn’t here. Instead, this is a collection of 10 horror games ordered by release date that we think are great for spooky season and beyond. Let us know in the comments what you would add to the list!

The cozy corner of the horror genre seems to have exploded overnight, and now tons of new slice-of-life horror games are in various stages of development. That said, the team behind newcomer The Village in the Shade is no stranger to the form; they made the Yomawari series, a cute-and-terrifying collection of creepy virtual tales. The Village in the Shade takes things back to the homestead, giving you (a child who emerged from a hole in the ground and was immediately given the responsibility of running an entire farm by yourself) the freedom to plant, sow, reap, ranch, and more. Just follow the important rules: don't go out at night, don't share secrets, and don't leave the village among others. You wouldn't want to break the rules, right? You could, theoretically, go about your idyllic rural living. But as you unravel the threads of what this village is, who you are, and why you're here, it's hard not to get drawn into the strange, mysterious, delightfully disturbing truths hiding in its shadows. Just don't forget to water your turnips before you go sneaking out again.

Fans of survival horror and old-school FMV adventure games will find plenty to love (and fear) in Tenebris Somnia. When a young woman visits her ex-boyfriend’s apartment and discovers he's trapped in a hellish dream world, it kicks off a well-executed survival-horror trek of inventive puzzles and resource management to overcome dangerous monsters. High-production, live-action cutscenes help tell the story of a deteriorating relationship and the toll an indie horror film took on its creators, and they play an important role in gameplay. Tenebris Somnia may not look like much due to its classic pixelated presentation, but its scares and story captivate. – Our Review

Resident Evil Requiem is not just one of the best Resident Evil games, but it’s also one of the best horror games ever made. It features a unique dual-protagonist structure. Grace Ashcroft is timid, new to the whole “shooting zombies in the head while dealing with Umbrella viruses” thing, and is generally just trying to do her job. Leon S. Kennedy, however, is a veteran of all that and more. Requiem splits its runtime between the two characters, letting you experience both sides of Capcom’s marquee survival-horror style. Grace’s sections leave your hands clammy and your blood pressure high as you desperately try to survive. Leon’s sections leave your hands shaking with adrenaline and your blood pumping with excitement as he mows down zombies (sometimes literally, courtesy of those pesky chainsaws). The result is a Resident Evil game that blends two typical RE experiences – terrifying and tough or exhilarating over-the-top action – into one cohesive package. It’s perfect for someone who wants to feel scared and then soon after receive the catharsis of being the one in control, like being the tragic victim who dies in Act One of the horror movie and the last one standing who lives to tell the tale. – Our Review

Little Nightmares developer Tarsier Studios has a knack for delivering creepy side-scrolling adventures, but Reanimal eschews any whimsy to become its scariest game yet. While mechanically it is similar to Little Nightmares and still puts small children in unimaginable peril, Reanimal is capital-H horror thanks largely to its terrifying threats and disturbing animal-themed imagery (this probably isn’t the game for animal lovers; some messed-up stuff happens to these critters). Escaping the game’s island setting is thrilling and chilling whether you’re playing alone or with a friend in co-op. Months after release, we’re still thinking about Reanimal’s memorable final sequence, which is worth the price of admission on its own. – Our Review

2001’s Silent Hill 2 is considered one of the best horror video games of all time for good reason. At release, it was a graphical powerhouse, using the PlayStation 2's horsepower to create a setting that begged to be explored, even though every bone in your body said you shouldn’t. The remake from developer Bloober Team took on a big task in modernizing the game without losing the original’s soul, and it did a great job. Among all the recent Silent Hill releases (Silent Hill f, Silent Hill: Townfall), the remake is our favorite. The story of James Sunderland and his troubling relationship with his departed wife is complex, emotional, and – important for the purposes of this list – unsettling and scary. – Our Review

Alan Wake 2 is an excellent pick for some spooky madness, in the vein of David Lynch’s seminal Twin Peaks mystery-surrealist series. Don’t worry too much about the “2” part of the game’s title. You just need to know that the titular Alan Wake character is a not-great writer who acts like he’s really great, his wife is missing, and he got trapped in the ambiguous Dark Place. He’s only one half of the Alan Wake 2 equation, with his segments set in a dream-like version of New York City. Playing as him feels the most Twin Peaks-y. The other half is Saga, a police officer who arrives in the Pacific Northwest town of Bright Falls to investigate a murder that might be linked to a cult. You can expect more traditional survival-horror gameplay from her. But this is still a Remedy Entertainment game, and without spoiling anything, it goes places. And along the way, you can expect plenty of scares. Turn the lights down low (or off), light a candle, and sit back and enjoy one of Remedy’s best games. – Our Review

Square Enix has gone two-for-two with its Paranormasight series, an anthology of stories about the strange and occult. And while the more recent Mermaid's Curse is a brilliant tale all its own, the first entry – The Seven Mysteries of Honjo – brings significantly more scares. A group of people in the city of Honjo find themselves caught in a spectral battle royale, using powerful objects and conditions to curse one another, with the allure of a prize at the end. Its magic isn't just in the flowchart timeline, where you can hop between different perspectives and protagonists to see how events play out from every angle, but also in the gorgeous stereoscopic environments and narrative puzzles. Adventure games are a classic genre, and Paranormasight will remind you of what the genre is capable of the moment you slowly spin your camera around, your eyes peeking out from behind your fingers.

Survival horror can contain multitudes, and as the years have worn on, the genre has grown to encompass a wide range of action-combat mechanics. Signalis feels like a re-centering in that respect. It's an isometric survival-horror indie project from developer rose-engine, filled with clever puzzles, scarce resources, limited inventory slots, and looming, oppressive dread. As the Replika unit Elster, you delve deep into a remote complex filled with horrors and monsters, searching for something, or someone, waiting down below. While love for classic horror games and other hallmarks of genre fiction will certainly draw you in, the stylish presentation and devastatingly human core will keep you forging ahead to the finale. Once you've breached the surface of Signalis' retro-future super-structures, you won't be able to turn back.

In horror movies, audiences often groan at a protagonist for putting themselves in seemingly grave danger just to learn more about a cursed amulet or bloodthirsty killer. But in Immortality, you are the protagonist, and despite a lingering sense that you shouldn't be digging into the archives of these abandoned films, each eerie new scene makes you want to dive deeper. It's a game about Marisa Marcel, an actress who almost starred in three movies in the late 20th century, but has since disappeared. None of the movies were ever released due to mysterious circumstances, but you have access to the archived, unedited live-action footage, including behind-the-scenes conversations. By scrubbing through footage, you can select people or items in each scene and jump to random footage from any other movie that includes the same person or item. The approach to puzzle-solving is unique and keeps you appropriately disoriented. The mystery at the center is an unsettling treat to unravel, and scary in new and unexpected ways. Immortality is one of a kind and an easy recommendation for horror fans who want to try something a little different.

In the decade since launch, Dead by Daylight has continued to succeed, thanks to a dedicated (and newcomer-friendly) fanbase and its towering roster of original and licensed personas from across pop culture horror. The asymmetrical multiplayer title has become an anthology of horror’s biggest faces, including Freddy Krueger, Ghostface, Pyramid Head, and even the Xenomorph. Whether you play as a Survivor, trying to escape all manner of nightmare locations through stealth and cunning, or as a Killer, whose experience feels more like a hunting club, you’ll understand why Dead by Daylight has become a recurring destination for fans of the gruesome and bizarre.

Read about the making of Dead by Daylight and how it sunk its teeth into millions of players in our six-page exclusive feature in Issue 368 (p. 42), available in our magazine archive to anyone with a free Game Informer account.

#4218. Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns Of The Patriots: Part 7 – Big Mama Mia | Super Replay

In 2008, Kojima Productions released what was billed as the swan song for Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear series: Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. The game had the staggering task of tying up decades of storytelling by bringing together Solid Snake, Ocelot, Otacon, Raiden, and many more characters for one explosive finale. The adventure centers on a rapidly aging Solid Snake racing against the clock to stop his twin and nemesis, Liquid Snake, one last time. Of course, there are far more bizarre shenanigans at play.

Guns of the Patriots was acclaimed for its storytelling, cinematic presentation, and evolution of the series' stealth gameplay, namely the OctoCamo suit that allowed Snake to mimic the appearance/texture of any surface he touched. It also has the distinct honor of earning a rare 10/10 review score from Game Informer. Now, thanks to the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2, we can finally revisit MGS 4 without dusting off a PlayStation 3.

Join recent Metal Gear convert Charles Harte, who will be on the sticks to experience Guns of the Patriots (via the Master Collection Vol. 2) for the very first time, alongside long-time series fan Marcus Stewart, who is revisiting MGS 4 for the first time in over a decade. The stream kicks off today live on Twitch and YouTube at 12 p.m. PT/3 p.m. ET, and will continue for two hours each week until we roll credits.

If you can't catch us live, you can watch each episode after they air by following the YouTube links below.

Every week, Game Informer editors enter the vault and dust off games from every genre and platform imaginable. Watch Replay to relive fond (and not so fond) memories from gaming’s past.

#4217. Marathon launch player numbers are about half those of the Server Slam, at least on PC

Marathon hasn't quite been able to attract the same volume of players the recent Server Slam did.

After a couple of delays, a plagiarism lawsuit, and at least one internal reboot, Bungie’s next big game has officially launched. Marathon, the extraction shooter from the studio behind Destiny, has managed to find a decent, if a little small of an audience.

The game’s player numbers on Steam are being compared to its recent free, open weekend, and not in a favourable manner.

Prior to Marathon’s launch, Bungie held a multi-day Server Slam, which offered anyone interested in playing the game a chance to try out almost all of its classes, two of its maps, as well as many of its gameplay and progression systems.

The open test was largely well-received, and players actually showed up for it. It peaked at a very respectable 143,621 concurrent players on Steam, which put it within striking distance of the peak concurrent of its chief competitor, Arc Raiders - at least when you compare both of their pre-launch Server Slam events.

In Arc Raiders’ case, those figures were far outpaced at the game’s actual launch, and the Embark shooter continues to command a very active player base to this day. A paid product garnering far more players than the same product’s own free sampler is never not a good sign, so many hoped something similar would happen with Marathon.

Marathon has now officially launched, and it doesn’t look like it managed to pull an Arc Raiders - at least so far. At its peak, the Bungie shooter attracted 88,337 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), which is a little over half of its Server Slam’s 143,621 peak concurrent.

Numbers have, of course, dropped since then, which is normal, as players log off for the night. This is obviously not the end of the road for Marathon. Friday, and the weekend, may well push numbers closer to the Server Slam heights.

Indeed, word of mouth is quite positive, with the game currently sitting at a Very Positive user review rating on Steam, based on over 4,600 reviews. As has been proven time and time again in recent years, nothing catapults a game like players emphatically advocating for it to their friends, so it could simply be that mainstream players are cautious.

It will become clear where things settle over the weekend.

#4216. Are You A Tired Parent? The Witcher 3's New Accessibility Mode Was Built With You In Mind

CD Projekt Red's director of player experience, Karolina Niewęgłowska, has taken to the company's official forum to explain the approach behind a new accessibility preset for The Witcher 3: Wild Hunt - Remastered (thanks, Push Square).

Dubbed 'Bard's Ballad', this option contains a number of individual accessibility toggles that you can tinker with to suit your own needs, or you can simply apply all of them at once as a blanket preset. So for example, this includes disabling item weight and durability along with the ability to disable herb icons on the mini-map.

Niewęgłowska explains that the option has been built for those who may have trouble concentrating, regardless of the underlying reason. It also considers players who may simply be feeling a bit tired, including parents. Here's what she had to say:

"Bard’s Ballad is for those having difficulty concentrating, including those with ADHD, or those experiencing cognitive fatigue, for example due to conditions like depression. But it’s also for folks who simply feel tired or overwhelmed in this busy world. A colleague to whom I described Bard’s Ballad said “so… a tired parent mode”. Very much so. But it is for anyone who wants to use it, to play in a way that fits their needs best."

Essentially then, Bard's Ballad is partially for those who only have limited time at the end of the day and don't want to faff about trying to find replacement weapons or managing inventory space.

"So you have an hour for yourself after a busy day managing a million topics, and you wanna play a game and focus on the story. You load your save, continue your quest, and your weapon immediately breaks. You have to figure out what to replace it with, and where you need to go to fix it. Then your inventory gets full. What to drop, what to sell, what to dismantle, what may be useful? That’s immersive to many people. But if you only have an hour at the end of your busy day, and have little energy left to manage and organise things, it may be the opposite of what you need. And Bard’s Ballad is addressing that."

Of course, as with all accessibility options, none of it is mandatory, so if you want to experience The Witcher 3 the way it was originally intended, you can do that (with stunning visuals and performance on the Switch 2, no less!). But it's really cool that developers are taking the time to think of those who might not, for whatever reason, be able to sink quite as much time into such a lengthy quest.

I have to say as someone with now mostly-grown kids and a few other afflictions, I appreciate hearing the developers talk like this (likely because they're in the same boat). It's hard to play big games, and when you do, you don't need it to be another job. Being able to turn of the parts that feel that way are a kindness. And the game you love is still there the way it always was if that isn't something you wish to use.

I think a lot of folks forget that early cheat codes were frequently vestigial "developer mode" settings for people whose time also wasn't free trying to test out the game.

I just wanted to say I feel very seen as the target audience for this! I typically only get 30-45 mins at the end of a long day, and it took me 6 months to play through the Witcher on the original Switch. This is genuinely a big push to replay the game, as inventory management became a big time sink as part of the experience. I hugely appreciate the amount of accessibility options CDPR include, others should take note.

In the end, I did not like my time with the game, but I applaud this kind of initiative. I kinda wish I knew about it, so I could turn off weapon and armor durability, I really don't like this mechanic

Wonderful! As a tired parent who expects to be so for another 2-5 years, I’ll probably take advantage of the inventory and item weight settings. I enjoy a balance of challenge and lack of tedium and repetitiveness, so I really appreciate the options being available, and I know I’m far from the only one!

I had a thought about a feature like this the other day, but rather than getting rid of the gameplay and let you focus on the story, it gets rid of the "stuffing", and let's you focus on the game.

120 hours game, enable this feature and it becomes 35 hours. Changes all of the progression to advance without pointless fetch quests/objectives. Makes all of the text and story elements more concise, no more pointless banter. Cuts out all the minigames, rewards come naturally through regular progression instead.

I really wanted this kind of feature when I was playing Final Fantasy 7 Rebirth. So much sidetracking and sidequests, felt like it didn't even have a main storyline.

I don't know on Switch 2, but on Series X and after the remaster, I noticed that the camera and combat don't make me dizzy anymore. I am finally starting to enjoy The Witcher 3 after 15 hours of slow-paced playthrough. I say this as a compliment because I guess it's not easy to tune a big and relatively old game like this for a larger audience.

I immediately turned off item durability and limited inventory weight. I've never liked those mechanics in games because it just leads to unnecessary busy work. I don't wanted added realism like that in my games. I play them to escape the monotony of the real world.

Great, now I want a game that features Geralt and Baby Mario.

When I was younger, I'd probably be like, "WHO NEEDS THIS!? Learn to play the game and get good". But then now that I'm old and have very little time to game, this sounds like a dream come true. The BEST part is that it still has the regular modes for people like me when I was a kid and wanted to master a game.

Wow. I don’t think I appreciated how much the immersion features in games are very much what turns me off from a lot of games!

Having tried and bounced off from so many Im Sims, that was very much the reason why! Fascinating addition yall!

That's great branding. I've long thought epic games like this should have an express mode where busy people can get the story and gameplay highlights for a third of the time. Those who have more money than time probably wouldn't mind paying full price for 1/3 of the gameplay.

If this was its own customized difficulty mode, I wouldn't have much of an issue, but calling it an "accessibility mode" definitely rubs me the wrong way.

I bounced right off Witcher 3 because of some of this stuff, looking forward to revisiting it with enhanced graphics and streamlined "immersion" fratures! 🥳

PS - it's odd to me how hung up some users here are about the word "accessibility." The idea is that these features make the game easier to get into for more people, not that you must have a disability to use them! ✌️

for example when you make healthcare or food more "accessible" to a population, it doesnt mean only for sick or starving people, it means more people get an opportunity to enjoy those things.

I am so in for this. My brother in law got me this game years ago and I feel a little bad for not finding the energy for it yet. Maybe it’s Bard to the rescue.

There was no immersion anyway as Geralt was totally definitely carrying 30 swords and 5 pairs of pants and an entire supermarket of food and...

I thought this was going censor bath scenes and unicorns

Nintendo is a bit notorious when it comes to lack of options. Really hope that it'll change in the future. Control schemes, full button mapping, UI stuff, fully skipping cutscenes, etc. etc.

Developers like CD Projekt Red and Nightdive Studios are showing the way forward.

As a tired parent, I will totally use these features on my next playthrough.

The feature that I found to be the most time-wasting was that weapons and armor are levelled, which makes you feel like you should be constantly upgrading your gear. And this really breaks immersion, too. Like, suddenly, Geralt is capable of using a slightly better sword that he couldn't use 5 minutes ago?

This is AWESOME and would have been welcome in both BOTW and TOTK.

I just don't have the patience for that kind of "weapon breaking / inventory management" stuff those games demand.

I TOTALLY get and respect the appeal of those facets in terms of immersion, etc. but being a "tired parent," with ADHD no less, this is so for me.

Wish more games would do stuff like this.

@-wc- people also forget that their life experience isn't the same as others, they may not have considered how people could have issues in this regard due to how they were born or something they've acquired in their lifetime (and I don't mean children here). It is admittedly odd given they had to scroll past people illustrating how it helps them with their disabilities, but what can you do?

@Joe11 personally, I have a vestibular condition which means gyro controls are something my brain simply can't process. There'll be reports of blizzards in hades before I start advocating for games to remove the feature or rename it to something disparaging simply because I don't use it though.

Reading this hits even harder given it’s currently 430am where I am, my daughter has done her fourth wake up tonight and I’m currently winding her back down with a bottle as I type this. All worth being tired for though <3

How about a "Make the game 6 hours long to complete mode"? That's the only way I'm in! I keep Elden Ring in the background as my "Lifetime Game". That means I hope to compete it within my maybe 30 years left to live. Not a joke.

I hope this sets a trend. I love to have a variety of accessibility options available.

I think this is great, but I wonder what convinced them to do this now. I've had ups and downs, and some of those downs have been extended periods of cognitive fatigue. There were times that even very simple games were too much. Some of those I was able to revisit and ended up loving and even mastering. But I know the situation they describe well. Not every game needs or benefits from such an accessibility mode, but narrative-heavy games with so-called immersive elements and an open world seem like they'd benefit the most from stuff like this. And by their nature, 3D action RPGs require significantly more time to accomplish things compared to older 2D games. These options sound like quite a good fit here.

I was already considering having a look at this game with how the remaster has been well received and because it sounds more appealing to me now than it did when it came out. These options just add to the appeal. There's another game with considerable accessibility modifiers that, so far, I haven't liked much. I may go back to it. Even though I haven't gotten on well with it, I've always praised the inclusion of those modifiers. It's good to see it.

Exceptionally thoughtful this and shows why this dev are a class above.

I’m knocking on 50 and love the idea of playing these games but with my aging brain I do feel overwhelmed with copious mechanics to remember and understand in some games so this feels like a great idea. I think I’ll give it another try soon (Zelda OoT first though and I can cope with the mechanics of that!).

@Joe11 "Accessibility" = make something accessible.Although it is very often referring to handicapped people, no wheelchair is mentioned in the definition.

@timp29 I thought so too. I approve of this but would also approve of that.

Shouldnt the wonders of AI be making us less tired? Seems like, as usual, technological advancements are having the opposite impact.

Accessibility = accessible isn't a serious argument. Do a Google search for the word accessibility, and every single result will be about making services usable by people with disabilities. The Gemini summary, plagiarized verbatim from Wikipedia: "Accessibility is the design of products, devices, services, vehicles, or environments to be usable by disabled people."

@-wc- I can explain the hang up. Accessibility is widely considered noble, precisely because it refers to removing access barriers for people with disabilities. But reviewers routinely appropriate this language to disparage games for not including unrelated customizations, in particular difficulty options.

That chafes beyond semantic concerns. Difficulty is a fundamental design element necessary to push gamers to engage with core gameplay systems, and using that strategy shouldn't be shamed by using disability-coded rhetoric.

You could say who cares, let the consumer do what they please with the product, but letting gamers skip the fundamental elements of the game's design does them a disservice. There was a very ironic negative review panning Mina the Hollower for being too difficult and not awarding trophies if you mod out the difficulty. The reviewer explained that he nerfed the settings at the first sign of friction and then had no fun because, for example, boss fights were mindless when you have infinite hp. He essentially never actually played the game and missed out on a really fun experience. (I wanted to link the article, but it looks like it was retracted.)

I hear what you are saying, but I already gave two examples of very common legitimate usage of "accessibility" that have nothing to do with being disabled. you are hung up on your connotations of the word.

I did the same google/ai search that you did, got the same answer. BUT, when I said "but accessibility is not just for disabled people" I got:

"You are completely right. Accessibility is fundamentally about universal design, meaning it is designed to be usable by everyone, to the greatest extent possible, without the need for adaptation."

you cant just take AI's first answer at face value and pretend it confirms your argument, objectively.

OTOH I have complex feelings about the nerfing of modern games. Mina the Hollower, yeah I flipped some of those switches specifically to make the game more playable for me i.e. more like a game I would enjoy playing. the game is still insanely reasonably hard, but I'm having more fun and I couldnt care less about trophies and badges or whatever.

But, the way Nintendo does it is consistently horrible, no matter what they try. IIRC in Mario Wonder, if your kid cant hang, they are FORCED to use yoshi for an easy mode even if they only want to play as Peach, for example. how is that fair to a 4 year old?

In another Mario game (maybe odyssey? cant remember) if you die like twice on a level it offers you invincibility or even to skip the entire level?! to me, thats too far and I think this is where we can agree.

@-wc- To be clear, I like customization options. Including difficulty options, and especially options like the ones described in this article. But they're about making a game more appealing to more people, not removing access barriers.

Tangential: your example demonstrates a risk of additional prompts when you don't like a LLM's first answer—many models seek to boost engagement through flattery and validation, e.g., "You are completely right." C.f., South Park s27e03.

"But they're about making a game more appealing to more people, not removing access barriers."

Frankly, this is a distinction without a difference.

I'm aware of AI pandering aka lying. I dont use it. ✌️

accessible = possibleappealing = desirable

The first is an issue of fairness, the latter is not.

indeed, but removing access barriers, as you say, makes the game more appealing to more people, wouldn't you agree? ☺️

Great! Any option to hide the nudity from the watchful eyes of my kids when I play besides "play a different game?"

#4215. Killing Floor 3 Studio Announces Layoffs After Publishing Hire Spree

Lauren has experience in the gaming and esports space, writing news, guides, features, reviews, lists, conducting interviews, and more. Before joining the team at DualShockers, Lauren was a Features Writer at Adventure Gamers, a Guides Writer at Gameranx, as well as contributing as a News Writer at PCInvasion and Daily

Layoffs are always devastating for the video game industry and the people affected. Unfortunately, they have become all too common, and whether it’s a small studio or a large household name, it seems nobody is safe in today’s climate.

Tripwire Interactive, best known for the Killing Floor series, is the latest studio to be hit by layoffs. The studio was founded back in 2005, and Embracer Group acquired Tripwire Interactive through its former subsidiary, Saber Interactive, in 2022.

In our Killing Floor 3 Review, we go over what could have worked and what didn't in the end for Tripwire's latest game.

In a statement published on the official Tripwire Interactive X account, the studio says it “has undergone a workforce reduction, affecting 36 talented people across our studio. This was certainly not an easy decision, but unfortunately, a necessary one for the organization.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

The team will continue to focus on Maneater 2, which was officially announced as part of Sony’s September State of Play. It’s expected to launch sometime in 2027.

As the name suggests, Maneater 2 is the sequel to 2021’s Maneater, an action-packed RPG where you are the biggest threat in the open-world oceans that you’ll traverse. There are new evolutions, discoveries to be made, and a whole lot of opportunities to become the villain.

It has also been confirmed that work will continue on Killing Floor 3, as the developers try to salvage the rocky start the game had when it was released back in July 2025. Killing Floor 3 reviews remain mixed among critics and players, and updates are still rolling out, containing new content and fixes.

This isn’t the first time this year that Tripwire Interactive has held layoffs. On March 4, the studio cut its workforce by 23 people, meaning this new round of layoffs brings Tripwire Interactive’s total this year to 59. Only time will tell if any of Tripwire Interactive’s projects will suffer from delays as a result of these layoffs.

Similar to this instance, a real reason wasn’t provided for the March 4 layoffs, instead citing: “As the gaming industry continues to evolve, so do the needs of our studios, which means understanding our long-term strategy and aligning with business realities where needed in order to stay focused on our key creative goals.”

Tripwire Interactive describes the impacted employees as “truly great people who are exceptional at their roles,” and vows to “help and support these individuals with compassion and dignity during transition.”

On November 4, 2026, Tripwire Presents, the publishing sector of Tripwire Interactive, announced that it would be expanding its business to include scaled publishing support for indie developers to help put the spotlight on indie titles from across a variety of genres. The purpose of the initiative is to provide greater visibility for self-published indie games that Tripwire believes fans will enjoy.

It has been confirmed that Tripwire Presents will continue to go ahead with their plans, and the games that have already been chosen are The Boss Gangster: Criminal Empire, Starforged Legacy, Mars Attracts, One-Eyed Likho, and Eslabong.

This round of redundancies adds another to the tally of alarmingly large video game industry layoffs just this year alone. Other examples include Sucker Punch making staff cuts shortly after the launch of the Complete Edition of Ghost of Yōtei, and, of course, the mass layoffs conducted by XBOX.

Another three rounds of XBOX layoffs are slated to begin this month and last into the new year.

#4214. Players Fear For Riftbound As New Legend Makes Up Huge Portion Of Tournament Meta

The Riftbound European Regional Championship just wrapped up in Stuttgart, Germany, and by all accounts, the event was a success for the game, but two distinct controversies over the weekend left a mark on the event for many players.

One involved a notoriously slow-playing participant who questioned the judges' quality and how the rules were implemented, while another was much larger in scale and related to the share percentage of certain Legends leading decks in the tournament. The latter point led to a final eight where two Legends accounted for seven decks, drawing comparisons to the domination of certain archetypes in Magic: The Gathering in recent years.

Update: As this story went live, game director Dave Guskin confirmed that Riftbound bans are due to be announced this Friday, with an effective date TBC.

The first flashpoint from the Riftbound ERC revolved around a player called Templar, who was accused on day one of deliberately slow-playing to run out the clock on opponents, so they could score points late in the game and leave opponents in a position where they couldn't respond.

Worse still, Templar reached a record 8-1, with time concerns in every match, before he was eventually disqualified from the event. There are some unsubstantiated rumors floating around on Reddit that Templar wasn't actually disqualified for his slow play, and it was instead for marking cards, another huge TCG no-no, but most players commenting on the situation believe it was for the slow play, and they're also demanding a follow-up punishment.

After Koko Lopez's ban last month, players are now calling for an example to be made of Templar, with a swift, long ban. If it's possible to prove that Templar was indeed intentionally slow-playing, and their deck was built for this exact purpose, we can see a reality where a ban is handed out, although it would likely be less than what was given to Koko Lopez, which was a much more flagrant breaking of long-standing rules and dishonesty.

Criticism is also being directed at the judges, who were asked to address pace-of-play issues in previous rounds, with players documenting how poorly some judges handled the situation and repeatedly warning Templar to speed up without taking formal action.

We can forgive Riot's mistakes just this once.

TCG metas are weird, but they come and go with every game. For Riftbound right now, Riven is a problem, and while card bans are expected soon to help address it before it develops further, the numbers from Stuttgart are telling. On day one, 126 decks were Riven decks; that's 43.3% of all decks at the event.

The number of Riven decks on day two fell to 47, but that was still 37% of the remaining field. Finally, in the top eight, four of the players were running Riven decks, meaning the percentage was back up to an even 50, and it just showcases the game in a negative light, because from the outside looking in, it appears as though there is little creativity in the strategy of the game, and players end up playing with cards they feel like they have to play with, rather than ones they want to play with. Ultimately, a Kennen player, Evanshrim, won the event; Kennen was the third most popular Legend at the event, with 44 total decks on day one. Outside of the top three Legends (Kai'sa being the remaining top three Legend) there were very few Legends with a meaningful following, and given how young the game is, that's quite disappointing. Riot will surely know this and will be working to balance the meta as soon as possible, especially with the first full year of tournaments now in the books, but the sooner these changes are implemented, the better.

#4213. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 30, 2026

Welcome to Devil's Night, the night before Halloween, where video games are best served scary. After tomorrow night – Halloween proper – no more scary video games allowed. At least not until mid-September, 2027. I'm sorry, I don't make the rules. Below you will find our weekend gaming recommendations (which is actually surprisingly light on scary games – apologies), but before that, here are some of the biggest stories of the week.

Phantom Blade Zero is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and it’s certainly one of the most impressive to watch. Beijing-based developer S-Game uses China’s Wuxia brand of action (which was actually banned for some time during the 20th Century by the country’s government) to create a stylish, fluid, and hyper-engaging combat system. It will constantly leave you in awe that action combat can look this good. But looks aren’t everything. Fortunately, Phantom Blade Zero delivers on all fronts, with weapon mechanics so detailed that picking up a new blade can feel like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. The story won’t blow your socks off, but it’s certainly engaging and enticing enough to bring you through Phantom Blade Zero’s 40 or so hours of content. If you’re not interested in the “perfect ending,” which is the only satisfactory one in my opinion, you can complete the game in less than 30 hours. S-Game mixes high-octane combat with sprawling and rewarding exploration to create a must-play during this already busy season of games. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Phantom Blade Zero review, and if you are hopping in this weekend, be sure to check out my list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks I wish I knew before starting it.

If you have any fond memories of IllFonic’s ill-fated Friday the 13th: The Game as I do, you simply must play the studio’s latest, Halloween: The Game. It is essentially Friday the 13th with Michael Myers instead of Jason, but with a decade of lessons learned from the team’s teeth carving in other horror properties and games. You’re either Michael or a citizen; the former wants to kill you and all the NPCs in various suburban maps, while the latter must rescue as many NPCs as possible while staying alive themselves. It’s that classic cat-and-mouse formula IllFonic is the master of, but with all the style, substance, and synths of John Carpenter’s Halloween masterpiece. Plus, Halloween: The Game features IllFonic’s first crack at a single-player campaign, and while it’s largely a tutorial for playing as Michael, if you’re a Halloween mega-fan like me, it’s worth checking out if only to take part in some of the film’s most iconic kills. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Halloween: The Game review here, and if you’re hopping in this weekend, there’s a new map, additional Halloween-themed cosmetics to unlock, and more waiting for you.

Overwatch is in the midst of its Halloween event, which have always historically been pretty interesting. This year it's Mystery Madness: Graveyard Games. In it, you begin by picking one of three characters in a random role. And then, as the game progresses, you choose perks that upgrade, alter, or completely change what your character can do. It can get really chaotic where by round three characters like Orisa might be three times her normal size or Torbjorn might have placed a giant turret on Mercy's making her a flying death machine. There are also Halloween skins, as well.

Tom the Postgirl is an odd little adventure that I'd recommend to fans of Untitled Goose Game. You play as Tom, a creepy girl who's tasked with delivering packages to the people of her wacky town, which is depicted with storybook-style illustrations and a color palette limited to black, white, and red. On the surface, you're delivering packages, but the game's real story is based on Tom's tendency to peep where she shouldn't, peering into townsfolks' windows to watch their odd lives. On house is full of kids who live like dogs; another has a couple with a bizarre obsession with tickling. You never know what each window might reveal, and I quickly sympathized with (and enabled) Tom's compulsion. You also have the capacity to cause quite a bit of trouble by stomping on flowers, haphazardly snipping strings and cords, or even stealing packages and using them for your own mischievous purposes. It's a pretty short experience, completable in just a few hours, making it a nice palate cleanser between the massive releases at the end of the year.

This Devolver Digital-published game has a simple but head-turning premise. You’re a profoundly angry woman who returns to her small hometown armed with nothing but a sledgehammer, which she uses to smash everything in sight. The town is also inhabited by robots possessing human consciousnesses. Swinging the hammer can either punch holes through walls or, with enough force, reduce entire buildings to rubble. But why is she doing this? Why is she so mad? A big part of Virtue and a Sledgehammer’s allure is its fascinating and well-written tale about the protagonist’s strained relationships with her sister and mother. Learning more about their lives requires you to keep smashing, but the more you learn, the more you begin to question whether smashing everything is actually a good idea.

This bizarre indie blends fun match-3 puzzle-solving with tower defense gameplay wrapped around a funny but surreal story. The match-3 gameplay involves sliding tiles to match geographic elements like castles, trees, and rivers to collect resources that feed into the tower defense portion. Depending on how the board looks when the puzzle portion ends, you send troops (sustained by the resources you collected) to attack/defend against rival castles and gather more items; board positioning determines how well this can go. The two mechanics feed into each other to create a fun loop that grows in complexity as new mechanics are introduced. Did I mention the game is also very weird? The silly tale centers on a medieval court designating you the chosen savior to rescue their lost queen (and many other tasks), and the dumb tone adds personality to a sometimes dry genre. Titanium Court charmed and impressed us when it launched on PC earlier this year, and now console and mobile players get their chance to hold court.

Sword of the Sea is a beautiful, 2025 game about surfing through the sand atop a floating sword. It recalls Journey, the emotional 2012 PlayStation game, which makes sense as it comes from the artists and developers that worked on that game, developer Giant Squid. Giant Squid also made 2016's Abzû and 2020's The Pathless. It's a talented team and Sword of the Sea maintains that reputation. And now you can play it on Switch 2. You can read my full review of the game (though this review pertains to the PlayStation 5 version) right here.

Cities: Skylines arrived on PC more than a decade ago, but is still revered as one of the greatest modern city-builders. Even now, three years after the sequel's release, Paradox continues supporting and porting the original game. A couple years after its initial release, Cities: Skylines received a strong console port, which did an admirable job of adapting the controls to gamepads, but the Switch version was always the weakest of the bunch. As of this week, Switch 2 owners can play a less compromised version, expanding the Switch's 9-tile limit to a much larger 25-tile limit, as well as better performance and textures, better control panels, and a ton of DLC and added content. And on top of that, if you own the Switch 1 version, you get a deep discount on the Switch 2 version.

While not specifically about this new Switch 2 version, you can read our original reviews of the base PC version here, and the base console version here.

Minecraft has held its dominant spot in pop culture for so long that it's easy to forget a simple fact about it: the game is awesome. This week, it's coming to Switch 2, giving potential miners another platform to explore procedurally-generated caves in. You've certainly heard of it, and you've probably played it, but I still feel it often doesn't get the flowers it deserves in high-level critical discussions about games, despite its regular cadence of major updates. The opening gameplay loop is so satisfying that for many of my peers, whether they regularly play video games or not, it's only a matter of time before they boot up a new world again. While you can never play the game for the first time again, if you haven't checked it out in a couple years, you might be surprised by the amount of new blocks, materials, and mobs they've added in recent updates. And if you've never played before, the Switch 2 launch is as good a time as any to see what all the fuss is about.

The card game incarnation of Arkham Horror remains one of the best narrative-driven and horror-themed tabletop games around, and it's an easy recommendation if you're looking for something engaging to dive into on Halloween night. Rooted in the monsters and mysteries of the Cthulhu Mythos, this living card game is built on major core sets and expansions. But unlike a TCG, each new installment has the same cards included, fueling the cooperative adventures you'll undertake together with your fellow players. Last year Arkham Horror: The Card Game did something of a soft relaunch for a chapter 2 of its narrative, and that new core set is an ideal place to jump on  play. Players each control an individual investigator as they explore arcane and weird mysteries, confront monsters, and unfold plots of cultists, ancient entities, and forbidden lore. For fans of cosmic horror storytelling, it's an easy pick.

#4212. Nioh 3 patch finally makes summons useful in boss fights, brings free armour for everyone

There's a new Nioh 3 patch out in the wild, and it's one that any player who regularly summons in boss fights will really appreciate.

Team Ninja continues to work on Nioh 3. The developer has been releasing regular updates for the action RPG since its launch in early February. Earlier patches have addressed major bugs like healing item use inconsistencies, and more have arrived since to tackle various balance and loot-related issues.

Today’s patch, version 1.04, is a major one, coming in at well over 1GB. There’s plenty here worth getting excited about, so let’s dig in.

To begin with, this is the patch that adds the promised free armour sets for both Ninja, and Samurai. When Nioh 3 reached one million sales, Team Ninja said it would gift every player the Thunderous set in celebration, and the set’s two variants are now available in-game.

The more interesting side of the patch is, unsurprisingly, its change log. There appears to be a focus on online co-op and AI summons in this one, with various tweaks to the make the process more rewarding, and, in some cases, worthwhile.

The amount of Glory obtained when you complete a mission in multiplayer has been increased, regardless of which player was the host. The other major change mainly affects AI Benevolent Grave summons, making it so bosses will no longer target a single player for almost the entirety of the fight.

While summoning AI helpers has always been useful in Nioh 3, they didn’t always help in boss fights, specifically because the boss tended to focus on the player who summoned them, leaving the AI to run around eating AoE hits before dying.

Patch 1.04 makes a couple of welcome gameplay tweaks to the feel of combat. Ninjutsu, and Onmyo Magic will now hit their targets more consistently in situations where there’s a difference in elevation between the player and the enemy.

In the same vein, you’ll now be able to attack (quick/strong) right after jumping, which removes the pause that previously buffered the attack instead. This could mean even more air combos that don’t specifically require Martial Arts.

You can look forward to a couple of quality of life tweaks in this patch, too, such as the change that allows the game to automatically send any Sudama Soul Cores dropped by merchants to your item box. This happens from the second one onwards, which means you won’t have to pick half a dozen each time you go to sell a batch of items.

Speaking of the item box, the limit of forging materials has been increased for some of them. If you’ve been running Battle Scroll missions and Expeditions for gear, you’ll be happy to know that you can now exit the session from the main menu directly.

There’s plenty more to patch 1.04, including fixes and balance tweaks for several weapons, such as Samurai dual swords, odachi, and more for a few Ninja weapons, too. The patch also brings several bug fixes to the game.

You can read the full set of patch notes on Steam.

#4210. Take Two Reveals How GTA 6 Hype Affected Previous Entries

Michael Manning (He/Him) has been enamored with video games since he first played the Sonic Classic Collection as a child. With decades of experience in gaming and a full tour as a Gaming Journalist, Michael is ready to step up to the plate. From AAA to the smallest passion projects, his motto is that every piece of ar

There are few franchises as synonymous with video games as Grand Theft Auto, an icon that has shone through every generation of gaming. From its humble beginnings as a pseudo-arcade car crasher to its modern form as a cinematic titan of industry, Rockstar has taken their simplest IP and carried it all the way to the stars.

Activision is drawing a line in the sand against third party lobby shopping apps, threatening bans outright.

With financial quarter stats coming through, more and more major companies are releasing info on their plans and recent successes. Take-Two is one such company, which recently celebrated a fantastic Q2 off the back of GTA 6’s hype.

Through their release, not only are the game’s preorder numbers much higher than they anticipated, but the rest of the series is soaking in the hype.

Take-Two separates different sectors of their gaming output, and standing alone in the examples for Core Existing IP is Grand Theft Auto. The hype for Grand Theft Auto 6 is almost indescribable, breaking through normal gaming’s walls and leaking into the wider public.

With all the hype, Take-Two has proudly revealed that other titles in the GTA franchise have been catching tons of attention, with eager players needing something to tide them over. GTA 4, GTA 5, and various other rereleases and remasters are in high demand as Grand Theft Auto fever runs rabid through Take-Two’s consumer base.

While the Grand Theft Auto series has always had anthology elements, rarely taking much from previous titles, Rockstar loves to slip small references and nods to their previous titles in. Between the burning need to play the game and the fear of missing out on any of its content, players are chomping at the bit for anything GTA-related that Take-Two is willing to put out.

From its humble beginnings as a pseudo-arcade car crasher to its modern form as a cinematic titan of industry, Rockstar has taken their simplest IP and carried it all the way to the stars.

Quoted directly from the report, GTA “exceeded our forecast ahead of next week’s eagerly anticipated launch of Grand Theft Auto VI,” and they’re not underselling. In the very rigid language of financial documentation, that means the larger GTA franchise has been selling like hotcakes.

It helps that previous titles genuinely hold up, a testament to Rockstar’s phenomenal dev work and even more reason to get excited. When people are hyped, all they want is more reasons to pump their fists. Take-Two has made it clear they’re absolutely willing to feed that flame, with an incredibly successful quarter behind them without even considering GTA 6’s launch sales.

With Grand Theft Auto buried in the larger cultural zeitgeist as deeply as it is, it’s no wonder Take-Two is going to try and use its success to double down, giving eager players all the GTA they want with the massive series behind them. I fully expect a Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas or Grand Theft Auto 4 Remake in the near future, bringing some of the fan-favorite old titles to modern standards.

With the incredible flexibility of Rockstar’s engines, they should be able to flip one around relatively quickly, though their perfectionism is a rule of nature at this point. Proper modern Steam ports of even older entries could also do well, as both San Andreas and 4 have Remasters on sale as we speak on Steam.

For now, Take-Two is refusing to rest on their laurels, a great sign for anyone who enjoys their massive selection. Between their various sports titles and the cultural icon that is Grand Theft Auto, they should never have to worry about money, allowing them to secure roles for their developers and work on smaller projects between their absolute moneymakers. The future is looking bright for Rockstar.

As GTA 6's launch approaches, everyone wants part of the PR pie, including internet ISPs.

#4209. Shigeru Miyamoto Proclaims November 1 is Pikmin Day, Pikmin 4 Demo Coming To Switch 2 Soon

This morning, Nintendo shared some updates related to the Pikmin franchise and has officially claimed November 1 as Pikmin Day, starting today and moving forward presumably forever.

Aside from the announcement of Pikmin Day as a general idea, Pikmin creator Shigeru Miyamoto appeared on camera to remind everyone that Pikmin 4 – Nintendo Switch 2 Edition + Dandori Academy is coming November 12. A free demo for the game, which will include one standard level and two Dandori Academy levels, will be available on November 2.

The Switch 2 version of the game (you can read Game Informer’s Pikmin 4 review here) will have improved visuals and take advantage of the Switch 2’s mic to let you say things like “Rush” and “Go to work” to Oatchi. The Dandori Academy side of the game is essentially time trials you can practice, and then on Fridays, Saturdays, and Sundays, you will have one chance to post your best time. You can read more about the Switch 2 version of the game here.

Miyamoto also shared that the mobile game, Pikmin Bloom, is also getting a fairly substantial update soon with secret caves. In Bloom, players will be able to find maps that reveal caves that you can send your Pikmin into to battle and find treasure. You can also find maps for Bloom by playing Pikmin 4. Caves will be coming to Pikmin Bloom later this year.

The Pikmin Day presentation also reminded viewers that every Pikmin game is available on Switch and Switch 2, though no announcements or hints were made implying that Pikmin 1 and 2 would be coming to the Nintendo Switch Online subscription service, which includes GameCube games on Switch 2. Those games can be purchased individually on the eShop.

Finally, Miyamoto brought actress Fuka Koshiba on the presentation (best known for voicing Kiki in Kiki’s Delivery Service) to share her appreciation for the Pikmin franchise (she likes to knit Pikmin hats that she shares on social media) and introduce a Pikmin short film. In the short, a Pikmin interacts with a toad, but I won’t spoil what happens. Miyamoto promised more shorts are on the way and in the future, they will be found in the Nintendo Today app.

Unfortunately, the stream concluded without a single reference to 2017's Hey! Pikmin. I wouldn't expect it to get a port to Switch 2 anytime soon.
